title: Wat Pa Mok, Ang Thong 2026 — Reclining Buddha & River Legend
metaDesc: Visit Wat Pa Mok Worawihan in Ang Thong, Thailand — a riverside temple on the Chao Phraya with a 22-metre gilded Reclining Buddha, the floating-Buddha legend, and the royal move that saved the statue from the eroding bank. Plus how to get there and where to eat nearby.

h1:
Wat Pa Mok Worawihan
Reclining Buddha by the Chao Phraya
intro: Wat Pa Mok Worawihan is an old riverside temple on the Chao Phraya that has been part of Ang Thong since the Ayutthaya period. The reason people come to pay respects is the Reclining Buddha, a gilded stucco statue more than 22 metres long inside its viharn. What really sticks in people's memory, though, is the floating-Buddha legend and the day King Thai Sa ordered the whole statue moved back from a riverbank the water was eating away. Here's what you'll find at the temple and how to make a day of it.

blocks.html: If you're driving along the Chao Phraya in Ang Thong, Wat Pa Mok is one temple worth a stop — not because it's huge or showy, but because its stories are so tightly tied to Ayutthaya history: the Buddha that supposedly floated downriver, the move that pulled the statue back from the eroding bank, and the visit by King Naresuan to pay respects here before heading off to war. The temple sits right on the water, the grounds are shady and cool, and you can stroll through it at an easy pace with no need to rush.

blocks.text: Where Wat Pa Mok is and how to get there

blocks.html: Wat Pa Mok Worawihan stands in Pa Mok subdistrict, Pa Mok district, Ang Thong province, on the bank of the Chao Phraya River. It's about 18 km from Ang Thong town, roughly a 20–25 minute drive. Coming from Bangkok takes about an hour and a half, and since it's very close to Ayutthaya, it pairs well into the same route.

items: Private car — the easiest option, with parking on the temple grounds. From Bangkok, take the Asia Highway (Route 32) and turn off into Pa Mok district.
Pair it with Ayutthaya — Pa Mok sits right next to Ayutthaya's northern edge, so it's only a short drive up from Ayutthaya. Perfect for a single day trip.
Songthaew or taxi from Ang Thong town — about 16–17 km, roughly 20 minutes. A good choice if you don't have your own wheels.

blocks.title: Best time to go
blocks.html: The temple is open for worship during the day, like most temples. Aim for morning to late morning — the sun isn't harsh yet, the light coming into the viharn is lovely, and the crowds are still thin. If you come in early October you'll hit the temple's annual festival, when it gets busier than usual.

blocks.text: The Reclining Buddha inside the viharn

blocks.html: The temple's highlight is the Reclining Buddha, a large statue enshrined inside the viharn. It's built of brick, coated in stucco and then lacquered and gilded all over, lying on its right side in the lion's-rest posture (sihasaiyas). Measured from the headpiece to the soles of the feet, it runs about 22 metres — one of the finest old reclining Buddhas of the Chao Phraya basin, in late-Ayutthaya style.

What many people love is the soles of the feet and the calm, still expression on the face. Visitors come to ask for blessings around peace of mind, work, and safe travels. The viharn stays cool and quiet inside; you can walk around the statue and take photos, but keep it respectful — this is a sacred place that locals have revered for a very long time.

items: Material — a brick core inside, coated in stucco, then lacquered and gilded all over
Posture — sihasaiyas, reclining on the right side with the head resting on the hand
Length — about 22 metres from the headpiece to the soles of the feet
Style — late Ayutthaya; the Fine Arts Department has restored and preserved it

blocks.text: The floating-Buddha legend and the royal move

blocks.html: The story that makes Wat Pa Mok memorable is the floating-Buddha legend. As it's told, the statue drifted down the Chao Phraya and came to rest, half-sunk, in front of the temple. Villagers held a ceremony and brought it ashore to enshrine on the riverbank, where it has been revered ever since.

The clearer chapter of history is the move itself. The Reclining Buddha's viharn originally sat right at the bank, until the river eroded so close that the statue was at risk. Around 1728, King Thai Sa of Ayutthaya ordered the whole Reclining Buddha pulled back from the riverbank — a distance of about a hundred-odd metres — and a new viharn built over it. Shifting an entire large stucco statue in that era was an extremely difficult feat of engineering, which is why the event was recorded in the royal chronicles.

Another story people pass down is that before King Naresuan the Great rode out to his elephant duel with the Burmese crown prince — a battle he won — records say he gathered his troops and paid homage to this very Reclining Buddha. That ties Wat Pa Mok into the history of Ayutthaya's fight for independence as well.

blocks.title: Where the name comes from
blocks.html: This spot was once two temples side by side — Wat Chi Pakhao and Wat Talat. They later merged into one and took the name Pa Mok, after the mok trees (a fragrant white-flowering tree) that grew thickly across the grounds.

blocks.text: What else to see around the temple

blocks.html: Beyond the Reclining Buddha's viharn, Wat Pa Mok has a few more spots to wander through at an unhurried pace. It sits right on the water, the grounds are leafy and shaded, and you can walk the whole temple in not much time.

items.name: Reclining Buddha viharn
items.blurb: The heart of the temple, enshrining the 22-metre gilded Reclining Buddha. Walk around the statue and ask for blessings.

items.name: The ordination hall (ubosot)
items.blurb: The temple's ordination hall, used for religious ceremonies, built in the style of an old royal temple.

items.name: Buddha-footprint mondop
items.blurb: A pavilion enshrining a stone-carved replica of the Buddha's footprint — another spot where people come to pay respects.

items.name: Chao Phraya riverfront
items.blurb: The riverside terrace in front of the temple — sit and catch the cool breeze, watch the boats pass and the river flow. An easy, relaxed spot.

blocks.text: Where to go after the temple

blocks.html: Wat Pa Mok makes a good pin on an Ang Thong temple route, since the province's famous temples are spread out not too far apart. You can drive on to the rest comfortably in a single day.

items: Wat Muang — the largest Buddha statue in Thailand and Ang Thong's signature photo stop, a short drive on from Pa Mok
Wat Khun Inthapramun — another old reclining-Buddha temple in Ang Thong; its statue is even longer and sits out in the open air
Ekkarat drum-making village — watch local craftspeople make drums and pick up handmade souvenirs
Boat noodles and roadside eats — Ang Thong is known for boat noodles and riverside food, so stop to refuel before moving on

blocks.title: Making the most of the day
blocks.html: If you have a full day, string together Pa Mok, Wat Muang and Wat Khun Inthapramun for a complete merit-making temple run, then cap it off with a bowl of Ang Thong boat noodles.

faq.q: How long is the Reclining Buddha at Wat Pa Mok?
faq.a: The Reclining Buddha in Wat Pa Mok's viharn measures about 22 metres from the headpiece to the soles of the feet. It's a brick-and-stucco statue, lacquered and gilded all over, in late-Ayutthaya style.

faq.q: What is the floating-Buddha legend of Wat Pa Mok?
faq.a: As the story goes, the statue floated down the Chao Phraya and came to rest, half-sunk, in front of the temple, so villagers held a ceremony and brought it ashore to enshrine. Later, around 1728, King Thai Sa ordered the statue pulled back from the bank the water was eroding — a distance of about a hundred-odd metres — and a new viharn built over it.

faq.q: How far is Wat Pa Mok from Ang Thong town?
faq.a: Wat Pa Mok Worawihan is in Pa Mok district, about 16–18 km from Ang Thong town, roughly a 20–25 minute drive. It's also close to Ayutthaya, so the two pair well into one route.

faq.q: Where can I go after visiting Wat Pa Mok?
faq.a: Ang Thong's famous temples sit close together. From here, continue to Wat Muang (Thailand's largest Buddha) and Wat Khun Inthapramun (an open-air reclining Buddha) for an easy single-day temple run.

faq.q: How is King Naresuan connected to Wat Pa Mok?
faq.a: The royal chronicles record that before King Naresuan the Great rode out to his elephant duel with the Burmese crown prince, he gathered his troops and paid homage to this very Reclining Buddha — tying the temple to that chapter of Ayutthaya history.
